Let the upper-left endpoint of the first slanted segment be \(A=(0,3)\), the common endpoint be \(U=(1,0)\), and the right endpoint of the second segment be \(B=(4,1)\).

Then
\[
\overrightarrow{UA}=(-1,3),\qquad \overrightarrow{UB}=(3,1).
\]
A \(90^\circ\) clockwise rotation sends \((x,y)\) to \((y,-x)\), so
\[
(-1,3)\longmapsto(3,1).
\]
Thus a \(90^\circ\) clockwise rotation about \(U\) maps \(A\) to \(B\) while fixing \(U\), and therefore maps the segment \(AU\) onto \(UB\).

For completeness, the only other possible endpoint correspondence would send \(A\to U\) and \(U\to B\). Its center would have to be the circumcenter of \(\triangle AUB\). Since
\[
\overrightarrow{UA}\cdot\overrightarrow{UB}=(-1)(3)+3(1)=0,
\]
the triangle is right-angled at \(U\), so its circumcenter is the midpoint of \(AB\), namely \((2,2)\). This point is not \(T,U,V,\) or \(W\).

Therefore, only \(U\) can be the center of the rotation.

\[
